subject: general
question: In some reptiles, the sex of the offspring is determined by:

options.text: Temperature at which eggs are incubated
Presence or absence of a Y chromosome

solution:
The correct answer is __**Temperature at which eggs are incubated**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In many **reptiles**, the sex of the offspring is not determined by **sex chromosomes** at the time of fertilization, but rather by the **environmental temperature** during **egg incubation**. This biological phenomenon is known as **Temperature-dependent Sex Determination (TSD)**.
 
• This process occurs during a specific window of **embryonic development** known as the **thermosensitive period (TSP)**. This period typically falls within the **middle third** of the total incubation time.
 
• The temperature experienced by the **developing embryo** during the **TSP** triggers physiological changes that determine whether the **gonads** will develop into **testes** or **ovaries**. ***Hence, the statement regarding temperature at which eggs are incubated is correct.***
 
• While most **mammals** and **birds** rely on **Genotypic Sex Determination (GSD)** involving **X, Y** or **Z, W chromosomes**, **TSD** is prevalent among various species of **turtles**, **crocodilians** (alligators and crocodiles), **tuataras**, and some species of **lizards**.
 
• Unlike **GSD**, where the sex ratio is usually **50:50**, **TSD** can lead to highly skewed sex ratios in a population depending on the **nesting environment** and **seasonal temperatures**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of TSD Patterns:**

 
 
• **Pattern Ia (MF):** In many **turtles**, **lower temperatures** during incubation produce **males**, while **higher temperatures** produce **females**.
 
• **Pattern Ib (FM):** In some **lizards** and **crocodilians**, the pattern is reversed, where **lower temperatures** result in **females** and **higher temperatures** result in **males**.
 
• **Pattern II (FMF):** In some species like **snapping turtles** and **crocodiles**, **females** are produced at both **extreme low and extreme high temperatures**, while **males** are produced at **intermediate temperatures**.
 
 
 
• **Biological Mechanism:**
 
 
• The conversion of **androgens** into **estrogens** is mediated by the enzyme **aromatase**. In species with **TSD**, the activity of this **enzyme** is often **temperature-sensitive**. **High temperatures** in certain species increase **aromatase activity**, leading to **ovary development** and **female offspring**.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with GSD:**
 
 
• In **Genotypic Sex Determination (GSD)**, sex is fixed by **DNA**. For example, in **humans**, the presence of the **Y chromosome** (specifically the **SRY gene**) determines **maleness**. In some **reptiles** like **snakes**, **GSD** is the primary method, often using the **ZZ/ZW system** where **females** are the **heterogametic sex (ZW)**.
 
 
 
• **Environmental and Evolutionary Impact:**
 
 
• **Climate change** poses a significant threat to species with **TSD**. Rising **global temperatures** can lead to an **overproduction of one sex** (e.g., nearly all **female sea turtles**), which could eventually lead to **population collapse** due to a lack of **reproductive partners**.
 
• **Ecological factors** such as **nest depth**, **shading from vegetation**, and **soil moisture** also play critical roles in regulating the **incubation temperature** within the **nest**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **pivotal temperature** is defined as the specific **incubation temperature** that produces an **equal ratio (50%)** of **males and females**. Even a small change of **1-2 degrees Celsius** can completely flip the **sex ratio** of a clutch.
 
• It is important to note that **hormonal levels in the mother** do not directly determine the **genomic or environmental sex** of the offspring in the same way **incubation temperature** does, although they can influence **egg quality**.
 
• **Reptiles** like **Green Sea Turtles** are classic examples where **warming sands** due to **global warming** are currently resulting in **extreme female bias** in hatchlings.
